stem: A delivery drone is flying in a straight line, descending at a constant speed of 12 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ along a path at 20° below the horizontal. It releases a package when the package is 35 m above level ground. Air resistance on the package is negligible unless stated.
diagramAlt: A drone moves down and to the right along a dashed straight path at an angle theta below the horizontal. At the moment of release the package has velocity v along the same direction. The height h of the package above the level ground is marked.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Show that the vertical component of the package's velocity at the moment of release is about 4 $\text{m s}^{-1}$.

parts.label: b
parts.question: Determine the time taken for the package to reach the ground.
markscheme: $35 = 4.10\,t + \tfrac{1}{2} \times 9.8 \times t^2$ (taking downwards as positive) ✓
OR final vertical speed $v_y = \sqrt{4.10^2 + 2 \times 9.8 \times 35} = 26.5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ ✓
solving for $t$, OR $t = \dfrac{v_y - u_y}{g}$ ✓
Allow ECF from (a); accept 2.21 to 2.36 s. Award [1 max] for $t = \sqrt{2h/g}$ = 2.67 s (initial velocity ignored).

mistakes.feedback: The package already has a downward velocity when it is released, so it reaches the ground sooner than a package dropped from rest.

parts.label: c
parts.question: Calculate the horizontal distance travelled by the package between release and landing.
markscheme: Allow ECF from (b); accept 24.7 to 26.9 m

mistakes.feedback: Only the horizontal component of the velocity carries the package sideways: use v cos θ, not v.

parts.label: d
parts.question: In practice, air resistance acts on the package. Outline how this affects the horizontal distance travelled by the package before it lands.
markscheme: Air resistance acts opposite to the package's velocity, so it has a horizontal component backwards / the horizontal velocity decreases during the fall ✓
so the package travels a smaller horizontal distance / lands closer to the point below the release point ✓

stem: An electric scooter starts from rest. The graph shows how its velocity changes with time during the first 12 s.
diagramAlt: Velocity in metres per second against time in seconds from 0 to 12, on a grid of 1 second by 1 metre per second squares. The curve starts at the origin, rises steeply, and bends over so that it levels off towards 12 metres per second. At 8 seconds the velocity is about 10.4 metres per second.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Describe how the acceleration of the scooter changes during the first 12 s.
markscheme: the acceleration decreases ✓
because the gradient of the graph decreases, approaching zero as the velocity approaches a constant value ✓

parts.label: b
parts.question: Estimate the distance travelled by the scooter in the first 8.0 s.
markscheme: the distance is the area under the graph from 0 to 8.0 s ✓
area estimated by counting squares (each square = 1 m) OR by splitting into strips/trapezia ✓
distance = 54 m ✓
Accept 50.1 to 58.9 m. Award [2 max] for ½ × 10.4 × 8.0 = 41.5 m (curve treated as a straight line).

mistakes.feedback: The graph is a curve, not a straight line: it lies above the straight line from the origin, so the area is larger than ½ × v × t. Count the squares under the curve.

parts.label: c
parts.question: Calculate the average acceleration of the scooter during the first 8.0 s.
markscheme: $a = \dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{10.4}{8.0} = 1.3\ \text{m s}^{-2}$; allow a velocity read from the graph between 10 and 11 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ ✓

parts.label: d
parts.question: Explain why the acceleration of the scooter just after it starts is greater than your answer to (c).
markscheme: the gradient of the curve (the tangent) is steepest at the start ✓
the average acceleration is the gradient of the straight line from the origin to the point at 8.0 s, which is less steep than the tangent at the start ✓

stem: Firefighters direct a jet of water from a hose. The water leaves the nozzle, which is at ground level, at a speed of 18 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ at an angle of 35° above the horizontal and lands on level ground. Each drop of water moves as a projectile. Air resistance is negligible unless stated.
diagramAlt: A hose nozzle on level ground points up and to the right. An arrow labelled u shows the velocity of the water leaving the nozzle at an angle theta above the horizontal, and a curved blue line shows the path of the water, which comes back down to the ground further along. Not to scale.

parts.label: a
parts.question: State the magnitude and direction of the acceleration of a drop of water at the highest point of its path.
markscheme: $9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ vertically downwards ✓

parts.label: b
parts.question: Show that the maximum height reached by the water is about 5.4 m.
markscheme: vertical component of the initial velocity $u_y = 18 \sin 35^{\circ} = 10.3\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ ✓
at the top $v_y = 0$, so $0 = u_y^2 - 2gH$ and $H = \dfrac{10.3^2}{2 \times 9.8} = 5.44\ \text{m}$ ✓
OR time to the top $= \dfrac{10.3}{9.8}$ s, then $H = u_y t - \tfrac{1}{2} g t^2$ ✓

parts.label: c
parts.question: Determine the horizontal distance from the nozzle at which the water hits the ground.
markscheme: time of flight $t = \dfrac{2 u_y}{g} = \dfrac{2 \times 10.3}{9.8} = 2.11\ \text{s}$ ✓
horizontal distance $= u \cos \theta \times t = 14.7 \times 2.11 = 31.1\ \text{m}$ ✓
Allow ECF from (b) if the time of flight is found from the maximum height; accept 30.1 to 32.0 m

mistakes.feedback: Only the horizontal component of the velocity carries the water along the ground: use u cos θ, not u.

parts.label: d
parts.question: Sketch, on the same axes, the path of the water with negligible air resistance and the path of the water when air resistance is significant. Label the two paths.
markscheme: the path with air resistance has a lower maximum height and a shorter horizontal range than the path without ✓
the path with air resistance is not symmetrical: it descends more steeply than it rises, so its highest point is nearer the landing point than the launch point ✓
Note: examiner's sketch (blue: negligible air resistance; orange: significant air resistance).
Accept a path without air resistance that is a symmetrical parabola; do not accept a path with air resistance that is symmetrical

parts.label: e
parts.question: Outline why air resistance reduces the horizontal distance travelled by the water.
markscheme: the resultant force on the water is no longer vertical: air resistance acts against the motion and so has a component opposite to the horizontal velocity ✓
the horizontal velocity is therefore no longer constant but decreases during the flight, so less horizontal distance is covered in each second ✓
air resistance also increases the downward deceleration on the way up, so the water does not rise as high and spends less time in the air ✓
Any 2 from the points above

stem: A wooden crate of mass 45 kg rests on a rough, horizontal concrete floor. A horizontal elastic cord of spring constant 1200 $\text{N m}^{-1}$ is attached to the crate and pulled so that its extension increases slowly. The crate stays at rest until the extension of the cord reaches 14.5 cm, when it starts to slide. The cord is then pulled so that the crate slides at constant velocity; the extension of the cord is now 11.0 cm. The cord obeys Hooke's law throughout.
diagramAlt: Side view of a wooden crate resting on a rough concrete floor. A horizontal elastic cord, drawn stretched, runs from the right side of the crate to a hand pulling it to the right. No forces are drawn. Not to scale.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Draw a free-body diagram of the crate while it slides at constant velocity.
markscheme: weight vertically downwards and normal force vertically upwards, drawn from the crate with equal lengths and labelled ✓
tension (pull of the cord) horizontally in the direction of motion and friction horizontally against it, with equal lengths and labelled ✓
Note: examiner's diagram.
Do not accept a forward "force of motion" or arrows that do not start on the crate; the horizontal pair should be noticeably shorter than the vertical pair

parts.label: b
parts.question: Calculate the force exerted by the cord on the crate at the moment it starts to slide.
markscheme: $F = k \Delta x = 1200 \times 14.5 \times 10^{-2}$ ✓

mistakes.feedback: The extension must be in metres before using F = kΔx: convert the centimetres.

parts.label: c
parts.question: Determine $\mu_d$, the coefficient of dynamic friction for the crate sliding on the concrete floor.
markscheme: at constant velocity the resultant force is zero, so friction $= $ tension $= 1200 \times 11.0 \times 10^{-2} = 132\ \text{N}$ ✓
normal force $= $ weight $= 45 \times 9.8 = 441\ \text{N}$ ✓
Accept 0.290 to 0.309. Award [2 max] for 0.39 (the extension at which sliding begins used: that gives the maximum static friction, not the dynamic friction)

mistakes.feedback: While the crate slides, the friction equals the pull at constant velocity, not the pull at the moment it started to move. Use the smaller extension.

parts.label: d
parts.question: Explain why the extension of the cord while the crate slides at constant velocity is smaller than its extension at the moment the crate starts to slide.
markscheme: the dynamic friction force is smaller than the maximum static friction force ✓
at constant velocity the tension equals the (smaller) dynamic friction, and by Hooke's law a smaller tension means a smaller extension ✓

parts.label: e
parts.question: A second identical crate is placed on top of the first. Predict, without calculation, the extension of the cord when the two crates slide together at constant velocity.
markscheme: the normal force doubles, so the friction doubles and the extension doubles to 22.0 cm ✓

stem: In a crash test, a car moving at constant velocity is stopped suddenly by a barrier. The head of the crash-test dummy in the driver's seat, of mass 4.5 kg, continues to move forwards until it strikes the airbag, which brings it to rest. The graph shows how the force exerted by the airbag on the head varies with time during the contact.
diagramAlt: Force in newtons against time in milliseconds, on a grid with small squares of 5 ms by 100 N and darker lines every 10 ms and 200 N. The curve is a smooth hump: zero at 0 ms, rising to a peak of about 1600 N at 30 ms, and falling back to zero at 60 ms. The time axis runs to 80 ms and the force axis to 2000 N.

parts.label: a
parts.question: The airbag exerts a force on the head. State the force that forms a Newton's third-law pair with this force.
markscheme: the force exerted by the head on the airbag, equal in magnitude and opposite in direction ✓

parts.label: b
parts.question: Estimate, using the graph, the impulse given to the head by the airbag.
markscheme: impulse $=$ the area under the force–time graph ✓
area estimated by counting squares (each small square $= 0.5$ N s) OR by strips/trapezia OR as about two-thirds of peak force $\times$ contact time ✓
impulse $= 61\ \text{N s}$ ✓
Accept 55.0 to 67.3 N s. Award [1 max] for $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 1600 \times 60 \times 10^{-3} = 48$ N s (hump treated as a triangle)

mistakes.feedback: The curve bulges above the straight lines from the ends to the peak, so the area is larger than that of a triangle. Count the squares under the curve, or use strips.

parts.label: c
parts.question: Determine the speed of the head just before it strikes the airbag.
markscheme: impulse $=$ change in momentum $= mv$, since the head is brought to rest ✓
Allow ECF from (b); accept 12.2 to 15.0 $\text{m s}^{-1}$

parts.label: d
parts.question: Without an airbag, the head would strike the steering wheel and be stopped in a much shorter time. Explain, with reference to the graph, how the airbag reduces the risk of injury to the head.
markscheme: the change in momentum of the head, and so the impulse, is the same whether it is stopped by the airbag or by the steering wheel ✓
the airbag increases the time over which the head is brought to rest ✓
since $F = \dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}$, the force on the head is smaller: the graph for the steering wheel would be a taller, narrower hump with the same area ✓

stem: An energy-storage scheme in a mountain valley links two reservoirs. At night, when the demand for electrical energy is low, pumps raise water from the lower reservoir to the upper one. During the day the water flows back down through turbines, which drive generators. The upper reservoir holds $1.2 \times 10^{6}$ $\text{m}^{3}$ of water of density 1000 $\text{kg m}^{-3}$, and the surface of this water is on average 320 m above the turbines. Pumping the full volume up takes 5.5 h with an electrical input power of 240 MW. Emptying the upper reservoir through the turbines takes 5.0 h and gives an average electrical output power of 190 MW.
diagramAlt: A mountain valley with an upper reservoir high on the left and a lower reservoir at the bottom right. A pipe runs from the upper reservoir down to a building housing the pumps and turbines next to the lower reservoir. The average height h of the upper water above the turbines is marked. Arrows show water pumped up at night and flowing down by day. Not to scale.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Show that the gravitational potential energy stored when the upper reservoir is full is about $3.8 \times 10^{12}$ J.
markscheme: mass of water $= \rho V = 1000 \times 1.2 \times 10^{6} = 1.2 \times 10^{9}\ \text{kg}$ ✓
$\Delta E_p = mg\Delta h = 1.2 \times 10^{9} \times 9.8 \times 320 = 3.76 \times 10^{12}\ \text{J}$ ✓

parts.label: b
parts.question: Calculate the average rate at which the water loses gravitational potential energy while the upper reservoir empties through the turbines.
markscheme: $P = \dfrac{\Delta E_p}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{3.76 \times 10^{12}}{5.0 \times 3600}$ ✓
Allow ECF from (a); accept 202 to 216 MW (the rounded value $3.8 \times 10^{12}$ J from (a) gives an answer about 1 % larger, inside this range)

mistakes.feedback: Power is energy per second: convert the time from hours to seconds.

parts.label: c
parts.question: Determine the overall efficiency of the scheme, defined as the electrical energy delivered by the generators as a percentage of the electrical energy used by the pumps.
markscheme: electrical energy in $= 240 \times 10^{6} \times 5.5 \times 3600 = 4.75 \times 10^{12}\ \text{J}$ ✓
electrical energy out $= 190 \times 10^{6} \times 5.0 \times 3600 = 3.42 \times 10^{12}\ \text{J}$ ✓
Accept 70.5 to 73.5 %. Award [2 max] for 91 % (generating stage only) or 79 % (pumping stage only)

mistakes.feedback: That compares the output with the energy stored in the water: it is the efficiency of the generating stage only. The question asks for electrical energy out over electrical energy in.
That is the efficiency of the pumping stage only (energy stored over electrical energy in). Compare the electrical energy out with the electrical energy in.

parts.label: d
parts.question: Outline what happens to the energy that is not returned to the electrical supply.
markscheme: work is done against friction and viscous forces as the water flows through the pipes, pumps and turbines (turbulence), so energy is transferred to the internal energy of the water and the pipes ✓
friction in the moving parts of the pumps, turbines and generators and the heating effect of the current in the windings and cables transfer energy to the surroundings as thermal energy ✓
the water leaving the turbines still has kinetic energy, which is not transferred to the generators ✓
Any 2 from the points above

parts.label: e
parts.question: The electrical energy in the region is generated mainly by wind and solar sources. Suggest why the storage scheme is valuable alongside these sources.
markscheme: the output of wind and solar sources depends on the weather and the time of day, so it cannot be adjusted to match the demand ✓

surplus electrical energy at times of high supply or low demand is stored as gravitational potential energy and most of it is returned quickly when demand exceeds supply, reducing the need for other generators and the wasting of the surplus ✓

stem: Heating buildings uses a large share of the energy supplied to homes in cold countries, and much of that energy escapes through the windows. On a cold day a room is heated to 20 °C while the air outside is at −8 °C. The window is a single pane of glass of area 1.8 $\text{m}^{2}$ and thickness 4.0 mm. Thin layers of almost still air cling to both faces of the glass, so the glass is much cooler than the room: its inside surface is at 5.4 °C and its outside surface is at 4.6 °C. The thermal conductivity of the glass is 1.0 $\text{W m}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$.
diagramAlt: Two cross-sections, not to scale. Left: a single pane of glass with the warm room on one side and the cold outside air on the other. Right: a double-glazed unit of two panes of glass with an air gap between them, again with the room on one side and the outside on the other.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Calculate the rate at which energy is conducted through the glass.
markscheme: $\Delta T = 5.4 - 4.6 = 0.8$ K (a temperature difference is the same in °C and in K) ✓
$\dfrac{\Delta Q}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{kA\Delta T}{\Delta x} = \dfrac{1.0 \times 1.8 \times 0.8}{4.0 \times 10^{-3}} = 360\ \text{W}$ ✓
Do not accept the air temperatures (giving $1.3 \times 10^{4}$ W).

mistakes.feedback: The temperature difference in the conduction equation is across the glass itself: use the temperatures of its two surfaces, not the air temperatures.

parts.label: b
parts.question: The surface temperatures stay roughly the same throughout a winter day. Estimate, in MJ, the energy transferred through the pane in one day.
markscheme: $E = P\Delta t$ with $\Delta t = 8.64 \times 10^{4}\ \text{s}$ (one day) ✓
Allow ECF from (a); accept 29.5 to 32.7 MJ, or the same value in J.

parts.label: c
parts.question: To reduce the energy loss, the window is replaced by a double-glazed unit: two panes of the same glass separated by a gap of width 12 mm filled with air. Compare the ways in which energy could be transferred across the air gap by conduction and by convection.
markscheme: conduction: energy is passed on through collisions between neighbouring molecules (faster molecules near the warmer pane transfer kinetic energy to slower ones) with no overall movement of the air ✓

convection: the air itself moves, because air warmed by the inner pane expands, becomes less dense and rises while cooler, denser air sinks, so a circulating flow of air carries the energy across the gap ✓

parts.label: d
parts.question: The thermal conductivity of air is 0.025 $\text{W m}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$. Explain why the double-glazed unit loses energy much more slowly than the single pane, for the same room and outside temperatures.
markscheme: the thermal conductivity of air is about 40 times smaller than that of glass, so for the same temperature difference the rate of conduction through a layer of still air is far smaller than through glass ✓
the gap is narrow, so the air cannot circulate freely and convection across the gap is largely suppressed / the air stays almost still, so energy must cross it mainly by (poor) conduction ✓
most of the temperature difference between inside and outside is now across the air gap rather than across the glass, so the rate of energy transfer through the whole unit is much smaller ✓

parts.label: e
parts.question: State one benefit to the environment of reducing the rate of energy loss from heated buildings.
markscheme: less fuel (or electricity generated from fuel) is needed for heating, so less carbon dioxide / greenhouse gas is released, reducing the enhanced greenhouse effect ✓
Accept less fossil fuel burned, or a reduction in any named pollutant from heating.

stem:
Venus orbits closer to the Sun than Earth does. At the orbit of Venus, sunlight delivers 2600 $\text{W m}^{-2}$ to a surface facing the Sun, and the thick clouds of Venus give it an albedo of 0.76. Spacecraft have measured the temperature of the surface of Venus to be 735 K. The atmosphere of Venus is almost entirely carbon dioxide, and the pressure at its surface is about 90 times the pressure at the surface of Earth.

For comparison, Earth would have an equilibrium temperature of about 255 K if it had no atmosphere; its actual surface temperature is 288 K.

parts.label: a
parts.question: State what is meant by the albedo of a planet.
markscheme: the ratio of the total power scattered (reflected) by the planet to the total power incident on it ✓
Accept "the fraction of the incoming radiation that is reflected back into space".

parts.label: b
parts.question: Venus is modelled as a black body with no atmosphere. Show that its equilibrium temperature would then be about 230 K.
markscheme: mean absorbed intensity $= \dfrac{I(1 - \alpha)}{4} = \dfrac{2600 \times (1 - 0.76)}{4} = 156\ \text{W m}^{-2}$ ✓

parts.label: c
parts.question: Explain why the surface temperature of Venus is so much higher than the temperature in (b).
markscheme: the surface of Venus radiates mainly infrared radiation, and carbon dioxide molecules absorb infrared photons whose energies match the differences between their (vibrational) molecular energy levels / resonate at those frequencies ✓
the molecules then re-emit this radiation in all directions, so a large part of it returns to the surface ✓
the surface receives energy from the atmosphere as well as from the Sun, so it must be at a higher temperature to radiate enough power to balance what it absorbs ✓

parts.label: d
parts.question: The surface of Venus has an emissivity of 1. Deduce the ratio of the energy emitted each second by one square metre of the surface at 735 K to the energy that the same square metre would emit each second at the temperature in (b).
markscheme: energy emitted per second per unit area $= \sigma T^4$, so ratio $= \left(\dfrac{735}{229}\right)^4$ ✓
ratio $= 106$ ✓
Allow ECF from (b); accept 101 to 111 (using 230 K gives 104).

parts.label: e
parts.question: Discuss what the measurements of Venus suggest about the enhanced greenhouse effect on Earth.
markscheme: Venus shows that a carbon dioxide atmosphere can raise a planet's surface far above its equilibrium temperature (by about 510 K, compared with about 33 K on Earth), so adding carbon dioxide to Earth's atmosphere by burning fossil fuels should be expected to raise Earth's surface temperature ✓
OR the measurements are evidence that the energy-balance model of the greenhouse effect is correct, because it accounts for a planet other than Earth

but the atmosphere of Venus is far denser and almost entirely carbon dioxide, so the comparison cannot say how much Earth warms for a given increase in carbon dioxide / Earth will not become like Venus because of human emissions alone ✓

stem: A sealed container at rest holds helium gas. Each helium atom has a mass of $6.64 \times 10^{-27}$ kg. The atoms move randomly, with a root-mean-square (rms) speed of 1.37 $\text{km s}^{-1}$. Helium behaves as an ideal monatomic gas.

parts.label: a
parts.question: State the average velocity of the helium atoms.
markscheme: zero: the atoms move equally in all directions, so their velocities (vectors) cancel ✓

parts.label: b
parts.question: Explain why the rms speed, rather than the average velocity, is used in the equation for the pressure of an ideal gas.
markscheme: the average velocity is zero, so it cannot describe how hard or how often the atoms hit the walls ✓
the momentum change in each collision and the rate of collisions both depend on the speed, so the pressure depends on the mean of the squares of the speeds, whose square root is the rms speed ✓

parts.label: c
parts.question: Determine the temperature of the helium.
markscheme: $\tfrac{1}{2}mv_{\text{rms}}^2 = \tfrac{3}{2}k_BT$ ✓
$T = \dfrac{mv_{\text{rms}}^2}{3k_B} = 301\ \text{K}$ ✓

mistakes.feedback: The average kinetic energy of an atom of an ideal monatomic gas is (3/2)kBT, not kBT.

parts.label: d
parts.question: The density of the helium is 0.16 $\text{kg m}^{-3}$. Calculate the pressure of the helium.
markscheme: $P = \tfrac{1}{3}\rho v_{\text{rms}}^2$ ✓
$P = \tfrac{1}{3} \times 0.16 \times (1.37 \times 10^{3})^2 = 1.0 \times 10^{5}\ \text{Pa}$ ✓

mistakes.feedback: P = (1/3)ρv²rms: remember the factor of one third.

stem:
A fixed mass of a monatomic ideal gas is taken round the cycle A → B → C → A shown on the graph.

  • A → B: the gas expands at a constant pressure of $2.0 \times 10^{5}$ Pa from $1.0 \times 10^{-3}$ $\text{m}^{3}$ to $2.0 \times 10^{-3}$ $\text{m}^{3}$.
  • B → C: the gas cools at constant volume.
  • C → A: the gas is compressed adiabatically back to A.
diagramAlt: Graph of pressure in units of 10 to the power 5 pascal against volume in units of 10 to the power minus 3 cubic metres. A horizontal line from A at volume 1.0 to B at volume 2.0, both at pressure 2.0. A vertical line down from B to C at volume 2.0 and pressure about 0.63. A curve rising steeply from C back to A.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Show that the pressure at C is about $6.3 \times 10^{4}$ Pa.
markscheme: $p_{\text{C}} = 2.0 \times 10^{5} \times \left(\dfrac{1.0 \times 10^{-3}}{2.0 \times 10^{-3}}\right)^{5/3} = 6.30 \times 10^{4}\ \text{Pa}$ ✓

parts.label: b
parts.question: Determine the thermal energy transferred to the gas during A → B.
markscheme: $W = p\Delta V = 200\ \text{J}$ ✓
$\Delta U = \tfrac{3}{2}p\Delta V$ (from $\tfrac{3}{2}nR\Delta T$ and $pV = nRT$) $= 300\ \text{J}$ ✓
$Q = \Delta U + W = 500\ \text{J}$ ✓

mistakes.feedback: That is only the work done by the gas. The internal energy of the gas also increases: Q = ΔU + W.

parts.label: c
parts.question: Determine the work done on the gas during C → A.
markscheme: $Q = 0$, so the work done on the gas equals the increase in internal energy ✓
$\Delta U = \tfrac{3}{2}(p_{\text{A}}V_{\text{A}} - p_{\text{C}}V_{\text{C}}) = 111\ \text{J}$ ✓
Allow ECF from (a); accept 106 to 116 J

parts.label: d
parts.question: Calculate the efficiency of this cycle.
markscheme: net work $= 200 - 111 = 89.0\ \text{J}$ (no work during B → C) ✓
Allow ECF from (b) and (c); accept 0.167 to 0.189

mistakes.feedback: Efficiency uses the NET work done by the gas over the whole cycle: subtract the work done on the gas during C → A.

parts.label: e
parts.question: Explain why the entropy of the gas does not change during C → A.
markscheme: No thermal energy is transferred to or from the gas during an adiabatic change ($Q = 0$) ✓
so $\Delta S = \dfrac{\Delta Q}{T} = 0$ (the change is treated as reversible) ✓

stem: A frost alarm uses a thermistor whose resistance increases as its temperature decreases. The thermistor is connected in series with a fixed resistor of resistance 2.2 $\mathrm{k\Omega}$ and a battery of emf 9.0 V with negligible internal resistance. An ideal voltmeter measures the potential difference across the thermistor, which controls the alarm.
diagramAlt: Circuit diagram: a battery of emf epsilon, a fixed resistor R and a thermistor in one series loop. A voltmeter V is connected across the thermistor, with a label saying its output goes to the alarm.

parts.label: a
parts.question: The fixed resistor is a metal resistor that stays at a constant temperature. State and explain whether it is an ohmic conductor.
markscheme: It is ohmic ✓
because at constant temperature its resistance is constant / the current in it is proportional to the potential difference across it ✓

parts.label: b
parts.question: At 0 °C the resistance of the thermistor is 3.3 $\mathrm{k\Omega}$. Calculate, in mA, the current in the circuit at this temperature.
markscheme: total resistance $= 2.2 + 3.3 = 5.5\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ ✓

mistakes.feedback: The thermistor and the fixed resistor are in series: use the total resistance.

parts.label: c
parts.question: Show that the potential difference across the thermistor at 0 °C is about 5.4 V.
markscheme: $V = IR_{\text{T}}$ OR $V = \dfrac{3.3}{5.5} \times 9.0 = 5.40\ \text{V}$ ✓

parts.label: d
parts.question: Calculate, in mW, the power dissipated in the fixed resistor at 0 °C.
markscheme: Allow ECF from (b); accept 5.65 to 6.13 mW

mistakes.feedback: That is the power in the whole circuit. Use the resistance of the fixed resistor only.

parts.label: e
parts.question: The alarm sounds when the potential difference across the thermistor is greater than 5.4 V. Explain why the alarm sounds when the temperature falls below 0 °C.
markscheme: As the temperature falls, the resistance of the thermistor increases (so the total resistance increases) ✓
so the current decreases and the potential difference across the fixed resistor ($IR$) decreases ✓
the emf is shared between the two components, so the potential difference across the thermistor increases above 5.4 V ✓

stem:
A cordless drill is powered by a rechargeable pack of lithium cells. To test the pack, a technician uses a variable resistor to draw a range of currents $I$ from it and measures the terminal potential difference $V$ of the pack at each current. The readings are shown in the table.

$I$ / A$V$ / V
2.019.5
6.018.5
10.017.5
14.016.5
18.015.5
diagramAlt: Empty axes for a graph of terminal potential difference V in volts, from 14 to 21 V, against current I in amperes, from 0 to 20 A, with a grid of 1 A by 0.5 V squares.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Draw, on the axes provided, a graph of $V$ against $I$ for the readings in the table, with a line of best fit.
markscheme: all five points plotted correctly, to within half a small square ✓
a single straight line of best fit through the points, extended to meet the $V$ axis ✓
Note: the examiner's graph:

plot.title: Axes for a graph of terminal potential difference V in volts against current I in amperes: I from 0 to 20 A and V from 14 to 21 V, with a grid of 1 A by 0.5 V

parts.label: b(i)
parts.question: Determine the emf of the pack.
markscheme: $\varepsilon$ = intercept on the $V$ axis (where $I = 0$) $= 20.0\ \text{V}$ ✓

parts.label: b(ii)
parts.question: Determine the internal resistance of the pack.
markscheme: Accept 0.230 to 0.270 Ω from a correctly drawn line, or the same value from $\varepsilon = I(R + r)$ with one pair of readings and the emf from (b)(i).

parts.label: c
parts.question: The pack is then fitted to the drill. Calculate the power delivered to the drill when the current is 14.0 A.

mistakes.feedback: The power delivered to the drill is the terminal p.d. (the p.d. across the drill) times the current, not the emf times the current: part of the emf is used inside the pack.

parts.label: d
parts.question: Explain, in terms of energy, why the terminal potential difference is lower at higher currents.
markscheme: the emf is the energy transferred to each coulomb of charge by the chemical reactions inside the pack, and it does not change ✓

some of this energy, $Ir$ per coulomb, is transferred to internal energy (heating) in the internal resistance of the pack, and this share grows as the current increases, so less energy per coulomb, $V = \varepsilon - Ir$, is delivered to the external circuit ✓

parts.label: e
parts.question: Outline why a pack of cells for a power tool should have a small internal resistance.
markscheme: a power tool draws a large current, so with a larger internal resistance the p.d. lost inside the pack ($Ir$) would be large and the terminal p.d., and so the power available to the motor, would fall sharply under load ✓
the power dissipated inside the pack, $I^2 r$, would be large, wasting the stored energy and heating the pack ✓

stem: A cylindrical fishing float of mass 24 g floats upright in still water. An angler pushes the float down a short distance and releases it, and it then bobs up and down with simple harmonic motion. The graph shows how its displacement $x$ from the equilibrium position varies with time. $x$ is measured downwards, so it is positive when the float is lower than its equilibrium position. Resistive forces are negligible.
diagramAlt: Graph of displacement x in centimetres against time in seconds, from 0 to 2.0 s, on a grid of 0.1 s by 0.5 cm. The curve is a cosine shape starting at its maximum of 2.0 cm at t = 0, crossing zero at 0.20 s, reaching −2.0 cm at 0.40 s and returning to 2.0 cm at 0.80 s and again at 1.60 s. Two and a half cycles are shown.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Determine, from the graph, the amplitude and the period of the oscillation.
markscheme: amplitude $= 2.0\ \text{cm}$ ✓
period $= 0.80\ \text{s}$ (one complete cycle, e.g. from the first peak at $t = 0$ to the next peak) ✓

parts.label: b
parts.question: When the float is at rest at its equilibrium position, the buoyancy force on it equals its weight. Explain why the motion of the float after it is released is simple harmonic.
markscheme: when the float is pushed below equilibrium it displaces more water, so the buoyancy force is greater than the weight and the resultant force is upwards, towards the equilibrium position (and when it rises above equilibrium the buoyancy force is less than the weight, so the resultant force is downwards) ✓
the extra buoyancy force equals the weight of the extra water displaced, $\rho g A x$, which is proportional to the displacement $x$ because the float is a cylinder of constant cross-section ✓
so the acceleration is proportional to the displacement and directed towards equilibrium / opposite to the displacement, which is the condition for SHM ($a = -\omega^2 x$) ✓

parts.label: c
parts.question: Calculate the maximum speed of the float.
markscheme: $\omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{T} = \dfrac{2\pi}{0.80} = 7.85\ \text{rad s}^{-1}$ ✓
Allow ECF from (a); accept 0.150 to 0.164 $\text{m s}^{-1}$

mistakes.feedback: The amplitude is in centimetres: convert it to metres before multiplying by ω.

parts.label: d
parts.question: Sketch a graph to show how the velocity of the float varies with time from $t = 0$ to $t = 1.6$ s. Label the maximum and minimum values of the velocity.
markscheme: a sinusoidal curve with the same period as the displacement graph (0.80 s), zero at $t = 0$ and at every half period (0.40 s) after that, covering two cycles ✓

the velocity is negative first (the float moves upwards after release, while $x$ is positive downwards), with the first minimum at $t = 0.20\ \text{s}$, and the maximum and minimum labelled $\pm$0.16 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ ✓
Allow ECF from (c) for the labelled values. Award [1 max] for a correct sine shape of the right period that is inverted (positive first).
Note: the examiner's sketch is shown below.

parts.label: e
parts.question: Determine the kinetic energy of the float when its displacement is 1.0 cm.
markscheme: $E_k = \tfrac{1}{2} m\omega^2 (x_0^2 - x^2) = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 24 \times 10^{-3} \times 7.85^2 \times \left[(2.0 \times 10^{-2})^2 - (1.0 \times 10^{-2})^2\right]$ ✓
OR $v = \omega\sqrt{x_0^2 - x^2} = 0.136\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ ✓ then $E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = 2.2 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{J}$ ✓
Allow ECF from (a) and (c); accept $2.08 \times 10^{-4}$ to $2.36 \times 10^{-4}$ J

mistakes.feedback: That is the potential energy at this displacement, ½mω²x². The kinetic energy is the total energy minus the potential energy: ½mω²(x₀² − x²).

stem: An earthquake produces P waves, which are longitudinal, and S waves, which are transverse. Both travel through the Earth's crust to a seismic station. In the crust, P waves travel at 6.0 $\text{km s}^{-1}$ and S waves at 3.5 $\text{km s}^{-1}$.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Outline the difference between the motion of particles of the crust when a P wave passes and when an S wave passes.
markscheme: P wave: particles oscillate parallel to the direction in which the wave travels (energy is transferred) ✓
S wave: particles oscillate perpendicular to the direction in which the wave travels ✓

parts.label: b
parts.question: The S wave arrives at the station 42 s after the P wave. Show that the station is about 350 km from the earthquake.

parts.label: c(i)
parts.question: The graph shows how the vertical displacement of the ground at the station varies with time as the S wave passes. Determine, in km, the wavelength of the S wave.
markscheme: period read from the graph: $T = 1.25$ s (or $f = 1/T$) ✓
$\lambda = vT = 3.5 \times 1.25 = 4.38\ \text{km}$ ✓
Accept 4.20 to 4.55 km

mistakes.feedback: Wavelength = speed × period (or speed ÷ frequency), not speed ÷ period.

parts.label: c(ii)
parts.question: State the total distance moved by a particle of the ground at the station during one period of the S wave.
markscheme: $4 \times 3.0 = 12\ \text{mm}$ ✓

mistakes.feedback: In one period the particle goes up and down and back again: four times the amplitude.

stem: A medical endoscope carries light into and out of a patient's body along a bundle of thin glass optical fibres. Each fibre has a core of refractive index 1.60 surrounded by a cladding of refractive index 1.50. The diagram shows one fibre. A ray of light in air meets the centre of the flat end face of the fibre with an angle of incidence of 25°. The end face is perpendicular to the axis of the fibre.
diagramAlt: A horizontal section of optical fibre: a core labelled n = 1.60 between two bands of cladding labelled n = 1.50, with a flat end face on the left. A ray in air comes from the upper left and meets the centre of the end face at 25 degrees to the dashed normal, which lies along the axis of the fibre.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Calculate the critical angle for light at the boundary between the core and the cladding.

mistakes.feedback: The boundary is between the core and the cladding, not between the core and air: use the ratio of the two refractive indices.

parts.label: b
parts.question: Determine whether the ray is totally internally reflected when it first reaches the boundary between the core and the cladding.
markscheme: $\sin\theta_2 = \dfrac{\sin 25^{\circ}}{1.60}$, so the angle of refraction in the core is $15.3^{\circ}$ ✓
the angle of incidence at the core–cladding boundary is $90^{\circ} - 15.3^{\circ} = 74.7^{\circ}$ ✓
$74.7^{\circ}$ is greater than the critical angle ($69.6^{\circ}$), so the ray is totally internally reflected / none of the light is refracted into the cladding ✓
Allow ECF from (a).

parts.label: c
parts.question: Sketch the path of the ray along a short length of the fibre, showing two reflections at the boundary between the core and the cladding.
markscheme: the ray bends towards the normal (towards the axis of the fibre) as it enters the core ✓
straight segments inside the core, reflected at the boundary with equal angles on the two sides of the normal, and no ray drawn in the cladding ✓
Note: the examiner's sketch is shown below.

parts.label: d
parts.question: In the bundle the fibres touch each other. Outline why each core is surrounded by a cladding of lower refractive index rather than being left as bare glass.
markscheme: where bare cores touched each other (or body tissue or fluid), the boundary would be between materials of similar refractive index, so there would be no critical angle (or a much larger one) and light would leak from one fibre into its neighbour ✓

the cladding keeps a boundary with a lower refractive index all the way along the core, so total internal reflection continues (and it protects the core surface from scratches and dirt, which would scatter light) ✓

parts.label: e
parts.question: Suggest one reason why optical fibres are well suited to viewing the inside of a patient's body.
markscheme: Any 1 from:
the fibres are thin and flexible, so a bundle can be passed along narrow, curved passages in the body ✓
light (and the image) is carried without any electric current or heating inside the body ✓
a view inside the body is obtained through a small natural opening or incision, so major surgery can be avoided ✓

stem: Two loudspeakers, S1 and S2, stand at one end of a school hall. They are connected to the same signal generator, which drives them in phase at a frequency of 425 Hz. A student walks slowly along a line parallel to the line joining the loudspeakers and notices that the sound is loud at some positions and very quiet at others. The point P on this line is 7.40 m from S1 and 5.40 m from S2. The speed of sound in the hall is 340 $\text{m s}^{-1}$.
diagramAlt: Plan view: a signal generator connected by wires to two loudspeakers S1 and S2, one above the other at the left. A dashed vertical line to their right is labelled as the line along which the student walks. A point P on this line is joined to S1 by a line labelled 7.40 m and to S2 by a line labelled 5.40 m.

parts.label: a
parts.question: State the condition for the two loudspeakers to act as coherent sources.
markscheme: the waves they emit have a constant phase difference / the same frequency and a constant phase relationship ✓

parts.label: b
parts.question: Calculate the wavelength of the sound in the hall.
markscheme: $\lambda = \dfrac{v}{f} = \dfrac{340}{425} = 0.800\ \text{m}$ ✓

mistakes.feedback: Wavelength = speed ÷ frequency, not frequency ÷ speed.

parts.label: c
parts.question: Determine whether P is a loud position or a quiet position.
markscheme: path difference $= 7.40 - 5.40 = 2.00\ \text{m}$ ✓
this is $2.5\lambda$ / an odd number of half wavelengths / $(n + \tfrac{1}{2})\lambda$ with $n = 2$ ✓
so the waves from the two loudspeakers interfere destructively at P, which is a quiet position ✓
Allow ECF from (b).

parts.label: d
parts.question: Explain why the sound at a quiet position is very faint even though both loudspeakers are emitting sound.
markscheme: the two waves arrive half a cycle out of phase / with a phase difference of $\pi$ (a compression from one loudspeaker arrives together with a rarefaction from the other) ✓

by the principle of superposition the displacements add to give a resultant of (almost) zero amplitude, so very little sound energy reaches the ear (not exactly zero, because the two waves have travelled different distances and so have slightly different amplitudes) ✓

parts.label: e
parts.question: The frequency of the signal generator is doubled. Predict, with a reason, what happens to the separation of neighbouring quiet positions along the line.
markscheme: the wavelength halves (to 0.400 m), because the speed of sound is unchanged ✓
neighbouring quiet positions differ in path difference by one wavelength, so they move closer together / their separation is roughly halved ✓

stem: An organ pipe of length 0.85 m has one closed end; its other end is open. Sound travels through the air inside it at 340 $\text{m s}^{-1}$.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Show that the wavelength of the first harmonic is about 3.4 m.
markscheme: a quarter of a wavelength fits the pipe (node at the closed end, antinode at the open end), so $\lambda = 4L = 4 \times 0.85 = 3.4\ \text{m}$ ✓

parts.label: b
parts.question: Calculate the frequency of the first harmonic.
markscheme: $f = \dfrac{v}{\lambda} = \dfrac{340}{3.4} = 100\ \text{Hz}$ ✓

mistakes.feedback: That is the first harmonic of a pipe open at both ends (λ = 2L). For a pipe closed at one end, λ = 4L.

parts.label: c
parts.question: Determine the frequencies of the next two standing waves that can form in this pipe, and state the harmonic number of each.
markscheme: next standing waves have $L = \tfrac{3\lambda}{4}$ and $L = \tfrac{5\lambda}{4}$ ✓
frequencies 300 Hz and 500 Hz ✓
these are the third and fifth harmonics (harmonic number = frequency ÷ first-harmonic frequency) ✓
Allow ECF from (b).

parts.label: d
parts.question: Explain why a standing wave of twice the frequency of the first harmonic cannot form in this pipe.
markscheme: there must always be a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end ✓
so the pipe length must be an odd number of quarter-wavelengths; twice the frequency would need L = λ/2 (two quarter-wavelengths), which would put a node at the open end ✓

parts.label: e
parts.question: The closed end is opened, so that the pipe is open at both ends. Calculate the new frequency of the first harmonic.
markscheme: antinodes at both ends, so $\lambda = 2L$ and $f = \dfrac{340}{2 \times 0.85} = 200\ \text{Hz}$ ✓

stem: Many stars belong to binary systems, in which two stars orbit their common centre of mass. The light from one star of such a system is analysed with a spectrometer. An absorption line of calcium, which has a wavelength of 393.40 nm when measured in a laboratory on Earth, is observed at a wavelength that changes with time. The graph shows the observed wavelength of this line over several days. Two times, A and B, are marked.
diagramAlt: Graph of observed wavelength in nanometres (393.30 to 393.50) against time in days (0 to 8), on a grid of 0.5 days by 0.01 nm. A dashed horizontal line marks 393.40 nm. The curve is a sine wave: it starts at 393.40 nm, peaks at 393.48 nm at 1.0 day (marked A), falls to 393.32 nm at 3.0 days (marked B), returns to 393.40 nm at 4.0 days and repeats, peaking again at 5.0 days and reaching its minimum at 7.0 days.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Outline why the observed wavelength of the line changes periodically.
markscheme: the star moves around its orbit, so the component of its velocity along the line of sight to Earth alternates between towards Earth and away from Earth ✓
the Doppler effect increases the observed wavelength when the star is receding and decreases it when the star is approaching, so the shift repeats once every orbit ✓

parts.label: b
parts.question: Determine the orbital period of the star.
markscheme: period $= 4.0$ days, e.g. from one peak to the next ✓

parts.label: c
parts.question: Calculate the maximum speed of the star along the line of sight.
markscheme: maximum shift $\Delta\lambda = 393.48 - 393.40 = 0.080\ \text{nm}$ ✓
$v = c\,\dfrac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda} = 3.00 \times 10^{8} \times \dfrac{0.080}{393.40} = 6.1 \times 10^{4}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ ✓
Accept $5.67 \times 10^{4}$ to $6.53 \times 10^{4}$ $\text{m s}^{-1}$ (allowing for the reading of the shift from the graph).

mistakes.feedback: The shift Δλ is measured from the laboratory wavelength to the peak (or the trough), not from trough to peak.

parts.label: d
parts.question: Deduce at which of the marked times, A or B, the star is moving towards Earth.
markscheme: at B the observed wavelength (393.32 nm) is shorter than the laboratory wavelength / the line is blueshifted ✓
a decrease in wavelength means the source is moving towards the observer, so the star is moving towards Earth at B (and away from Earth at A) ✓

parts.label: e
parts.question: State one assumption that must be made if the speed found in (c) is to be taken as the orbital speed of the star.
markscheme: the orbit is seen edge-on from Earth / the line of sight lies in the plane of the orbit, so at A and B the whole of the star's velocity is along the line of sight ✓
OR the orbit is circular, so the orbital speed is constant ✓

stem: A satellite of mass 850 kg is in a circular orbit 600 km above the surface of the Earth. Its engines are used to move it to a circular orbit 2400 km above the surface. The mass of the Earth is $5.97 \times 10^{24}$ kg and its radius is $6.37 \times 10^{6}$ m.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Show that, in the first orbit, the satellite moves at about 7.6 $\text{km s}^{-1}$.
markscheme: $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{r}} = 7.56\ \text{km s}^{-1}$ ✓

parts.label: b
parts.question: Calculate the period of the satellite in the first orbit.
markscheme: $T = \dfrac{2\pi r}{v}$ ✓
Allow ECF from (a); accept 5620 to 5970 s

mistakes.feedback: The satellite goes round a circle whose radius is measured from the centre of the Earth, not from the surface.

parts.label: c
parts.question: Deduce that the total energy of a satellite of mass $m$ in a circular orbit of radius $r$ is $E = -\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$.
markscheme: $E_{\text{k}} = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \dfrac{GMm}{2r}$ (using $v^2 = GM/r$) ✓
$E = E_{\text{k}} + E_{\text{p}} = \dfrac{GMm}{2r} - \dfrac{GMm}{r} = -\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$ ✓

parts.label: d
parts.question: Determine the minimum energy that the engines must supply to move the satellite to the second orbit.
markscheme: $\Delta E = \dfrac{GMm}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{r_1} - \dfrac{1}{r_2}\right)$ ✓
$\Delta E = 4.98 \times 10^{9}\ \text{J}$ ✓
Allow ECF from (a) and (c); accept $4.78 \times 10^{9}$ to $5.19 \times 10^{9}$ J. Award [2 max] for the change in potential energy only, $9.97 \times 10^{9}$ J.

mistakes.feedback: That is the gain in gravitational potential energy only. The satellite also loses kinetic energy: use the change in total energy.

parts.label: e
parts.question: The engines supply energy to the satellite, yet its kinetic energy is smaller in the second orbit. Explain this.
markscheme: In a higher orbit the orbital speed is lower, so the kinetic energy ($GMm/2r$) decreases ✓
the gravitational potential energy ($-GMm/r$) increases by twice as much as the kinetic energy falls, so the total energy increases and the engines must supply the difference ✓

stem: Titan and Rhea are moons of Saturn. Each moves in an approximately circular orbit. Titan has an orbital radius of $1.22 \times 10^{9}$ m and an orbital period of 15.9 days. Rhea has an orbital radius of $5.27 \times 10^{8}$ m.

parts.label: a
parts.question: A moon of mass $m$ orbits a planet of mass $M$ in a circle of radius $r$ with period $T$. Deduce that $T^2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2}{GM}r^3$.
markscheme: the gravitational force provides the centripetal force: $\dfrac{GMm}{r^2} = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$ ✓
with $v = \dfrac{2\pi r}{T}$ ✓
so $\dfrac{GM}{r^2} = \dfrac{4\pi^2 r}{T^2}$, which rearranges to $T^2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2}{GM}r^3$ ✓

parts.label: b
parts.question: Determine the mass of Saturn.
markscheme: period in seconds: $T = 15.9$ days $= 1.37 \times 10^{6}\ \text{s}$ ✓
$M = \dfrac{4\pi^2 r^3}{GT^2} = 5.69 \times 10^{26}\ \text{kg}$; allow ECF from (a) ✓

mistakes.feedback: Convert the period to seconds before using T² = 4π²r³/(GM).

parts.label: c
parts.question: Calculate, in days, the orbital period of Rhea.
markscheme: $\dfrac{T_{\text{R}}^2}{r_{\text{R}}^3} = \dfrac{T_{\text{T}}^2}{r_{\text{T}}^3}$ (OR using the mass from (b)) ✓
$T_{\text{R}} = 15.9 \times \left(\dfrac{5.27 \times 10^{8}}{1.22 \times 10^{9}}\right)^{3/2} = 4.51$ days ✓

parts.label: d
parts.question: Explain why the masses of the moons are not needed in (b) and (c).
markscheme: the moon's mass cancels (it appears on both sides of the force equation), so the orbital period does not depend on it ✓

stem: An electrostatic precipitator removes smoke particles from the waste gas leaving a factory chimney. Inside the chimney, two large vertical metal plates are 0.30 m apart and the potential difference between them is 60 kV. The gas flows upwards between the plates. A smoke particle of mass $5.0 \times 10^{-13}$ kg, carrying a negative charge of magnitude $8.0 \times 10^{-16}$ C, enters the gap next to the negative plate.
diagramAlt: Two large vertical metal plates seen edge-on, the left one labelled negative and the right one labelled positive, with the separation marked below them and the potential difference labelled above. A small smoke particle is drawn just to the right of the negative plate, and a dashed arrow between the plates shows the flue gas flowing upwards.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Sketch, on a copy of the diagram, the electric field lines between the plates and two equipotential surfaces. Ignore edge effects.
markscheme: at least four straight, parallel, evenly spaced field lines at right angles to the plates, with arrows pointing from the positive plate to the negative plate ✓
two equipotential surfaces drawn as straight lines parallel to the plates, at right angles to the field lines ✓
Note: examiner's figure.

parts.label: b
parts.question: Calculate the electric field strength between the plates.

mistakes.feedback: The potential difference is given in kilovolts: convert it to volts first.

parts.label: c
parts.question: State the work done by the electric field on the particle when the particle moves along one of the equipotential surfaces you have drawn.
markscheme: zero ✓

parts.label: d
parts.question: Determine the work done by the electric field on the particle as it moves from the negative plate to the positive plate.
markscheme: $W = q\Delta V_e$ ✓
Allow the answer in electronvolts: $3.0 \times 10^{8}$ eV. Accept $4.65 \times 10^{-11}$ to $4.95 \times 10^{-11}$ J.

mistakes.feedback: W = qΔV uses the potential difference between the plates, not the field strength.
The potential difference is in kilovolts: convert it to volts.

parts.label: e
parts.question: In practice the particle does not keep accelerating all the way to the positive plate. Explain, with reference to the forces acting on the particle, why it soon moves towards the plate at a constant speed.
markscheme: Any 2 from:
the electric force $qE$ on the particle is constant because the field is uniform ✓
the drag force from the gas on the particle increases as its speed increases ✓
when the drag force becomes equal (and opposite) to the electric force the resultant force is zero, so the speed stays constant (a terminal speed) ✓
Allow the weight to be ignored: it is much smaller than the electric force.

parts.label: f
parts.question: Outline one environmental benefit of fitting the precipitator to the chimney and one limitation of what it can achieve.
markscheme: benefit: smoke / soot / ash particles are attracted to the plate and removed from the gas before it leaves the chimney, so less particulate pollution reaches the air (fewer breathing problems, less soiling of the surroundings) ✓

limitation: only charged particles are collected, so gases such as carbon dioxide or sulfur dioxide pass through unchanged OR a high-voltage supply (electrical energy) is needed to run it OR the collected ash must still be disposed of ✓

stem: Two long straight parallel wires, P and Q, are 6.0 cm apart in air. P carries a current of 15 A and Q carries a current of 5.0 A in the same direction.
diagramAlt: Two long vertical wires, P on the left and Q on the right, 6.0 cm apart. Arrows show that both currents flow upwards: 15 A in P and 5.0 A in Q.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Calculate the magnetic field strength due to P at the position of Q.
markscheme: $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$ with $r$ in metres ✓
$B = \dfrac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 15}{2\pi \times 6.0 \times 10^{-2}} = 5.0 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{T}$ ✓

mistakes.feedback: Convert the distance to metres: 6.0 cm = 0.060 m.

parts.label: b
parts.question: Determine the force on each metre of wire Q.
markscheme: $F = BIL$, so $\dfrac{F}{L} = BI_{\text{Q}}$ (OR $\dfrac{F}{L} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi r}$) ✓
$\dfrac{F}{L} = 5.0 \times 10^{-5} \times 5.0 = 2.5 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{N m}^{-1}$; allow ECF from (a) ✓

parts.label: c
parts.question: Outline how the force on P compares with the force on Q, in both magnitude and direction.
markscheme: the forces are equal in magnitude, even though the currents are different (Newton's third law) ✓
they are in opposite directions: each wire is attracted towards the other, because the currents are in the same direction ✓

parts.label: d
parts.question: At one point on the line between P and Q, the resultant magnetic field due to the two wires is zero. Determine the distance of this point from P.
markscheme: between the wires the two fields are in opposite directions, so $\dfrac{\mu_0 I_{\text{P}}}{2\pi x} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_{\text{Q}}}{2\pi (d - x)}$ ✓
$\dfrac{15}{x} = \dfrac{5.0}{6.0 - x}$, so $x = 4.5\ \text{cm}$ from P ✓

stem: A student releases a short bar magnet from rest so that it falls, north pole first, through a coil of 500 turns and cross-sectional area 8.0 $\text{cm}^{2}$. The coil is connected to a data logger that records the emf induced in it. At the moment of release the centre of the magnet is 6.0 cm above the centre of the coil. The graph shows how the induced emf varies with time after the release.
diagramAlt: Graph of emf in volts against time in milliseconds from 0 to 180 ms, on a grid of 10 millisecond by 0.05 volt squares. The emf is zero at first, then dips to a negative pulse that reaches about minus 0.32 volts near 95 milliseconds, crosses zero at about 111 milliseconds, rises to a taller, narrower positive pulse of about plus 0.42 volts near 127 milliseconds, and returns to zero by about 160 milliseconds.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Outline the main features of the graph.
markscheme: the emf is zero while the magnet is far from the coil, then there is a negative pulse as the magnet enters the coil followed by a positive pulse as it leaves, after which the emf returns to zero ✓
the second pulse has a greater peak value and lasts for a shorter time than the first ✓

parts.label: b
parts.question: Explain why the second pulse has the opposite sign to the first, and why it is taller and shorter.
markscheme: the flux (linkage) through the coil increases as the magnet enters and decreases as it leaves, and by Lenz's law the induced emf (current) opposes each change, so the emf reverses direction ✓
the magnet is accelerating under gravity, so it is moving faster when it leaves the coil than when it enters ✓
the flux therefore changes at a greater rate, giving a larger emf (Faraday's law), and the same change in flux takes less time, so the pulse is shorter ✓

parts.label: c
parts.question: Estimate, using the graph, the change in the magnetic flux linkage of the coil while the magnet enters it, that is during the first pulse.
markscheme: the change in flux linkage $N\Delta\Phi$ is the area between the first pulse and the time axis (since $\varepsilon = -N\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$) ✓
area ≈ 20 squares × 0.50 $\text{mV s}$ per square, so $N\Delta\Phi \approx 0.010\ \text{Wb}$ ✓
Accept $8.50 \times 10^{-3}$ to 0.0115 Wb, by counting squares or using strips; ignore the sign.

parts.label: d
parts.question: Calculate the average magnetic flux density over the area of the coil when the centre of the magnet is at the centre of the coil.
markscheme: flux through one turn $\Phi = \dfrac{N\Delta\Phi}{N} = \dfrac{0.010}{500} = 2.0 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{Wb}$ ✓
Allow ECF from (c); accept 0.0212 to 0.0288 T.

mistakes.feedback: Your estimate in (c) is the flux linkage of all the turns. Divide by the number of turns to get the flux through one turn before dividing by the area.

parts.label: e
parts.question: The magnet is now released from a greater height above the coil. Predict, with a reason, how the graph changes.
markscheme: both pulses have greater peak values and are narrower (shorter), because the magnet is moving faster as it passes through the coil, so the flux changes at a greater rate and in a shorter time ✓
Allow: the area under each pulse is unchanged because the total change in flux is the same.

stem: A low-pressure sodium lamp used for street lighting contains sodium vapour. When a current flows in the vapour the lamp gives out light whose spectrum is a line spectrum, almost all of it in a single yellow line. The diagram shows the ground state and three excited energy levels of a sodium atom.
diagramAlt: Energy-level diagram with four horizontal lines. From the bottom: the ground state at minus 5.14 electronvolts, level 1 at minus 3.04 electronvolts, level 2 at minus 1.95 electronvolts and level 3 at minus 1.39 electronvolts. A blue downward arrow from level 1 to the ground state is labelled transition for part b.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Outline how the line spectrum of the lamp provides evidence that the energy of a sodium atom can take only certain discrete values.
markscheme: only certain wavelengths / frequencies / photon energies are present in the light ✓

a photon is emitted when the atom moves from one energy level to a lower one, with energy equal to the difference between the levels ($E = hf$), so only certain energy differences, and hence only certain levels, can exist ✓

parts.label: b
parts.question: Calculate, in nm, the wavelength of the photon released in the transition shown by the arrow on the diagram.
markscheme: $\lambda = \dfrac{hc}{\Delta E} = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34} \times 3.00 \times 10^{8}}{3.36 \times 10^{-19}} = 592\ \text{nm}$ ✓
Accept 580 to 604 nm.

mistakes.feedback: That is the wavelength for the transition from level 3 to the ground state. The arrow shows level 1 to the ground state.

parts.label: c
parts.question: Deduce which transition between the levels shown gives the photon of shortest wavelength, and the number of different photon energies that transitions between the levels shown can produce.
markscheme: level 3 to the ground state, because it has the largest energy difference and so the highest frequency / shortest wavelength ✓
6 different photon energies ✓

parts.label: d
parts.question: White light is sent through a tube of sodium vapour at room temperature. Describe how the absorption spectrum produced differs in appearance from the emission spectrum of the lamp.
markscheme: dark lines on a continuous bright background, instead of bright lines on a dark background ✓

the dark lines are at the same wavelengths as (some of) the emission lines OR only the lines for transitions starting from the ground state appear, because the cool atoms are almost all in the ground state ✓

parts.label: e
parts.question: The same yellow line appears as a dark line in the spectrum of the Sun. State what this tells astronomers.
markscheme: sodium is present in the Sun (in its outer layers / atmosphere) ✓

stem: In an experiment on the photoelectric effect, monochromatic light falls on a metal surface. For each frequency $f$ of the light, the stopping voltage $V_{\text{s}}$ is measured: the smallest potential difference that stops all the emitted electrons from reaching the collecting electrode. The graph shows the results.
diagramAlt: Graph of stopping voltage in volts against frequency in units of 10 to the 14 hertz, from 4 to 11. Five measured points lie on a straight line that meets the frequency axis at 5.5 and rises to 2.0 volts at 10.5 and 2.2 volts at 11.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Below a certain frequency, no electrons are emitted however bright the light is. Outline why this observation supports a particle model of light rather than a wave model.
markscheme: In the wave model, energy arrives continuously, so bright enough light of any frequency should eventually release electrons ✓
In the photon model, each electron absorbs the energy of one photon, $E = hf$; below the threshold frequency one photon has less energy than the work function, whatever the number of photons ✓

parts.label: b
parts.question: State the threshold frequency of the metal.
markscheme: $f_0 = 5.5 \times 10^{14}\ \text{Hz}$ (the intercept on the frequency axis) ✓

parts.label: c
parts.question: Determine, using the graph, a value for the Planck constant.
markscheme: $eV_{\text{s}} = hf - \Phi$, so the gradient of the graph is $\dfrac{h}{e}$ ✓
gradient read from the line, e.g. $\dfrac{2.0 - 0}{(10.5 - 5.5) \times 10^{14}} = 4.0 \times 10^{-15}\ \text{V s}$ ✓
Accept $6.20 \times 10^{-34}$ to $6.60 \times 10^{-34}$ J s. Do not accept the data booklet value without a gradient.

mistakes.feedback: The gradient of the graph is h/e, not h: multiply it by the elementary charge.
That is the data booklet value. The question asks for the value this experiment gives: use the gradient of the graph.

parts.label: d
parts.question: Calculate the minimum energy, in eV, needed to remove an electron from this surface.
markscheme: $\Phi = hf_0$ ✓
$\Phi = 2.20\ \text{eV}$ ✓
Allow ECF from (b) and (c); allow the data booklet value of $h$ (giving about 2.3 eV); accept 2.08 to 2.32 eV

parts.label: e
parts.question: The intensity of the light is doubled while its frequency stays the same. Explain the effect, if any, on the stopping voltage.
markscheme: No change in the stopping voltage ✓

The maximum kinetic energy of the electrons depends only on the photon energy ($hf$) and the work function; more intense light means more photons per second, so more electrons per second, not more energetic electrons ✓

stem:
A small modular nuclear reactor is planned to supply electrical power to a town. It will deliver 80 MW of electrical power with an overall efficiency of 33%. The fuel is enriched in uranium-235. One of the many fission reactions that occur in the reactor is

$$^{1}_{0}\text{n} + {}^{235}_{92}\text{U} \rightarrow {}^{140}_{54}\text{Xe} + {}^{A}_{Z}\text{X} + 2\,{}^{1}_{0}\text{n}$$

Each fission frees, on average, 200 MeV of energy.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Deduce the nucleon number A and the proton number Z of the nuclide X.
markscheme: nucleon number conserved: $A = 1 + 235 - 140 - 2 = 94$ ✓
proton number (charge) conserved: $Z = 92 - 54 = 38$ ✓

parts.label: b
parts.question: Estimate the number of fissions per second in the reactor and hence the mass of uranium-235 that undergoes fission each day.
markscheme: thermal power from fission $= \dfrac{80\ \text{MW}}{33\%} = 242\ \text{MW}$ ✓
fissions per second $= \dfrac{242 \times 10^{6}}{3.20 \times 10^{-11}} = 7.6 \times 10^{18}\ \text{s}^{-1}$ ✓
mass per day $= 7.6 \times 10^{18} \times 86400 \times 235 \times 1.661 \times 10^{-27} = 0.26\ \text{kg day}^{-1}$ ✓
Accept 0.3 kg from rounded intermediate values. Award [2 max] if the efficiency is not used (electrical power taken as the fission power).

parts.label: c
parts.question: Explain why the reactor needs a moderator.
markscheme: the neutrons released by fission are fast (have high kinetic energy), and uranium-235 is much more likely to undergo fission when it absorbs a slow (thermal) neutron ✓
the moderator slows the neutrons, through repeated collisions with its (light) nuclei, so that enough neutrons cause further fissions and the chain reaction is sustained ✓

parts.label: d
parts.question: Outline how the control rods are used to keep the power output of the reactor steady.
markscheme: the rods absorb neutrons, so they are moved further into the core to reduce the number of neutrons available for fission (and withdrawn to increase it) until, on average, one neutron from each fission goes on to cause another ✓

parts.label: e
parts.question: Discuss one advantage and one problem of supplying the town from this reactor rather than by burning fossil fuels.
markscheme: advantage: no carbon dioxide (greenhouse gas) is released while generating OR only a very small mass of fuel is needed (high energy density, as in (b)) OR a steady supply that does not depend on the weather ✓

problem: the fission products are highly radioactive and some stay hazardous for thousands of years, so the waste must be stored securely for a very long time OR the risk of an accident releasing radioactive material OR security / proliferation concerns, public acceptance or high cost ✓

stem:
In the core of a red giant, helium nuclei fuse to form carbon:

$3\,{}^{4}_{2}\text{He} \rightarrow {}^{12}_{6}\text{C}$

The mass of a helium-4 atom is 4.002603 u and the mass of a carbon-12 atom is 12.000000 u.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Calculate, in u, the decrease in mass in one reaction.

parts.label: b
parts.question: Show that the energy released in one reaction is about 7.3 MeV.

parts.label: c
parts.question: The red giant has a luminosity of $4.0 \times 10^{29}$ W. Assume that all of this power comes from this reaction. Calculate the number of reactions per second in the core.
markscheme: luminosity is the power radiated, so reactions per second $= \dfrac{L}{E}$ with $E$ in joules ✓
$N = \dfrac{4.0 \times 10^{29}}{7.27 \times 10^{6} \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19}} = 3.4 \times 10^{41}\ \text{s}^{-1}$; allow ECF from (b) ✓

mistakes.feedback: Convert the energy per reaction from MeV to joules (1 MeV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ J) before dividing.

parts.label: d
parts.question: Explain why the fusion of helium requires a higher core temperature than the fusion of hydrogen.
markscheme: helium nuclei have twice the charge of protons, so the electrostatic repulsion between them is greater ✓
so the nuclei need greater kinetic energy (a higher temperature) to get close enough for the strong force to act and fusion to happen ✓

parts.label: e
parts.question: Two stars end their lives leaving remnant cores of 1.2 solar masses and 1.8 solar masses. Outline, with reference to the Chandrasekhar and Oppenheimer–Volkoff limits, what each core becomes.
markscheme: the 1.2 solar mass core is below the Chandrasekhar limit (about 1.4 solar masses) ✓
so electron degeneracy pressure supports it and it becomes a white dwarf ✓
the 1.8 solar mass core is above the Chandrasekhar limit but below the Oppenheimer–Volkoff limit, so it becomes a neutron star (supported by neutron degeneracy pressure) ✓

stem: A hospital cyclotron accelerates protons, which move in a circle in a uniform magnetic field of strength 1.5 T. The protons spiral outwards as they gain energy and leave the cyclotron when the radius of their path is 0.40 m. They then strike a target and produce the radioactive isotope fluorine-18, which is used in medical scans.

parts.label: a(i)
parts.question: Show that the speed of the protons when they leave the cyclotron is about $5.7 \times 10^{7}$ $\text{m s}^{-1}$.
markscheme: $qvB = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$ (magnetic force provides the centripetal force) ✓

parts.label: a(ii)
parts.question: Explain why the magnetic field does not change the kinetic energy of the protons.
markscheme: the magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity (direction of motion) ✓
so it does no work on the protons ($W = Fs\cos 90^{\circ} = 0$): it changes their direction but not their speed ✓

parts.label: a(iii)
parts.question: Calculate the time taken by a proton to complete one circle in the magnetic field.
markscheme: $T = \dfrac{2\pi r}{v} = \dfrac{2\pi m}{qB}$ ✓
Award both marks for $2\pi r/v$ with the values from (a)(i).

parts.label: a(iv)
parts.question: Calculate, in MeV, the kinetic energy of a proton when it leaves the cyclotron.
markscheme: $E_{\text{k}} = 17.2\ \text{MeV}$; allow ECF from (a)(i) ✓

parts.label: b(i)
parts.question: Calculate the Lorentz factor $\gamma$ for the protons when they leave the cyclotron.
markscheme: $\dfrac{v}{c} = 0.19$, so $\gamma = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}} = 1.019$; allow ECF from (a)(i) ✓

parts.label: b(ii)
parts.question: Comment on whether it was reasonable to use $E_{\text{k}} = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$ in (a)(iv).
markscheme: $\gamma$ is only about 2 % greater than 1 ✓
so the relativistic correction to the kinetic energy is only a few per cent: the non-relativistic equation is a reasonable approximation ✓

parts.label: c(i)
parts.question: The half-life of fluorine-18 is 110 min. Calculate the decay constant of fluorine-18, in $\text{s}^{-1}$.
markscheme: $\lambda = \dfrac{\ln 2}{110 \times 60} = 1.05 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{s}^{-1}$ ✓

mistakes.feedback: Convert the half-life to seconds before using λ = ln 2 / T½.

parts.label: c(ii)
parts.question: At the end of production the activity of the fluorine-18 is $5.0 \times 10^{10}$ Bq. It takes 45 min to transport the sample to a hospital. Determine the activity of the sample when it arrives.
markscheme: $A = A_0 e^{-\lambda t}$ with $t = 45 \times 60$ s ✓
$A = 3.77 \times 10^{10}\ \text{Bq}$; allow ECF from (c)(i) ✓

mistakes.feedback: The transport time is less than one half-life, so the activity falls by less than half: use A = A₀e^(−λt).

parts.label: c(iii)
parts.question: Calculate the number of fluorine-18 nuclei in the sample when it arrives.
markscheme: $N = \dfrac{A}{\lambda}$ ✓
$N = 3.59 \times 10^{14}$; allow ECF from (c)(i) and (c)(ii) ✓

parts.label: d(i)
parts.question: The beam of protons hitting the target is equivalent to a current of 50 $\mu\text{A}$. Show that the beam delivers energy to the target at a rate of about 860 W.
markscheme: number of protons per second $= \dfrac{I}{e} = \dfrac{50 \times 10^{-6}}{1.60 \times 10^{-19}}$ ✓
$P = \dfrac{I}{e} \times E_{\text{k}} = 861\ \text{W}$ (OR $P = IV$ with $V$ = 17.2 MV) ✓

parts.label: d(ii)
parts.question: The target is cooled by water, which warms by 12 K as it flows past. Water has a specific heat capacity of 4200 $\text{J kg}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$. Calculate the mass of water that must flow past the target each second.
markscheme: $P = \dfrac{m}{t}c\Delta T$ ✓
$\dfrac{m}{t} = 0.0171\ \text{kg s}^{-1}$; allow ECF from (d)(i) ✓

stem: A tram stores energy in a flywheel, a uniform disc of mass 300 kg and radius 0.40 m that spins about its central axis. The moment of inertia of a uniform disc is $I = \tfrac{1}{2}MR^2$. At full speed the flywheel rotates at 3000 $\text{rev min}^{-1}$.
diagramAlt: A uniform disc of mass M seen face on, with its radius R drawn from the centre to the edge and a curved arrow showing it spinning with angular speed omega about its centre.

parts.label: a(i)
parts.question: Show that the moment of inertia of the flywheel is about 24 $\text{kg m}^{2}$.

parts.label: a(ii)
parts.question: Calculate the rotational kinetic energy of the flywheel at full speed.
markscheme: $\omega = \dfrac{3000 \times 2\pi}{60} = 314\ \text{rad s}^{-1}$ ✓
$E_{\text{k}} = \tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2 = 1.18 \times 10^{6}\ \text{J}$; allow ECF from (a)(i) ✓

mistakes.feedback: Convert the rotation rate to an angular speed in rad s⁻¹: multiply revolutions per second by 2π.

parts.label: a(iii)
parts.question: The tram is parked and the flywheel is left spinning freely from full speed. The only torque on it is a constant frictional torque of 0.80 $\text{N m}$ in the bearings. Determine the time taken for the flywheel to stop.
markscheme: $\alpha = \dfrac{\tau}{I} = 0.0333\ \text{rad s}^{-2}$ ✓
$t = \dfrac{\omega}{\alpha} = 9420\ \text{s}$; allow ECF from (a)(i) and (a)(ii) ✓

parts.label: a(iv)
parts.question: Calculate the number of revolutions the flywheel makes while it slows down to rest.
markscheme: $\Delta\theta = \dfrac{\omega_{\text{i}} + \omega_{\text{f}}}{2}t$ (OR $\omega_{\text{i}}^2 = 2\alpha\Delta\theta$) ✓
number of revolutions $= \dfrac{\Delta\theta}{2\pi} = 2.36 \times 10^{5}$; allow ECF from (a)(iii) ✓

parts.label: b
parts.question: The flywheel is used to accelerate the tram, of mass $1.8 \times 10^{4}$ kg, from rest to 6.0 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ on level track. During this time the flywheel slows from 3000 $\text{rev min}^{-1}$ to 2400 $\text{rev min}^{-1}$. Determine the efficiency of this energy transfer.
markscheme: energy given up by the flywheel $= \tfrac{1}{2}I(\omega_1^2 - \omega_2^2) = 4.26 \times 10^{5}\ \text{J}$ ✓
kinetic energy gained by the tram $= \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = 3.24 \times 10^{5}\ \text{J}$ ✓
$\eta = \dfrac{3.24 \times 10^{5}}{4.26 \times 10^{5}} = 0.76$; allow ECF from (a)(i) ✓

mistakes.feedback: Use the energy the flywheel actually gave up (from the change in its rotation rate), not all the energy it stored.

parts.label: c(i)
parts.question: The flywheel turns a rectangular generator coil of 200 turns and area 0.020 $\text{m}^{2}$ in a uniform magnetic field of strength 0.35 T. The coil turns at the same rate as the flywheel at full speed. Determine the average emf induced while the coil turns through a quarter of a revolution, starting from the position where the flux linkage is greatest.
markscheme: change in flux linkage $= NBA$, in a time of a quarter of a period, $\dfrac{1}{4f}$ with $f = 50\ \text{Hz}$ ✓
$\varepsilon = \dfrac{N\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t} = 4NBAf = 280\ \text{V}$ ✓

parts.label: c(ii)
parts.question: Explain how the emf from the generator changes as the flywheel slows down.
markscheme: the flux linkage changes more slowly, so the peak (maximum) emf decreases ✓
and its frequency decreases: each cycle of the emf takes longer ✓

parts.label: c(iii)
parts.question: Explain, with reference to Lenz's law, why the flywheel slows down more quickly when the generator supplies a current.
markscheme: the induced current opposes the change that produces it, so the forces on the coil produce a torque opposing the rotation ✓
the electrical energy supplied comes from the kinetic energy of the flywheel (energy is conserved), so it loses energy faster ✓

parts.label: d(i)
parts.question: Explain, in terms of the particles of the steel, why the bearings warm up as the flywheel slows down.
markscheme: work done against friction transfers energy to the bearings ✓
increasing the random kinetic energy of the particles of the steel, so the internal energy and temperature increase ✓

parts.label: d(ii)
parts.question: The bearings and their steel housing have a total mass of 45 kg. Steel has a specific heat capacity of 450 $\text{J kg}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$. Calculate the rise in temperature of the bearings and housing when the flywheel runs down from full speed to rest, assuming no energy leaves them.
markscheme: $Q = mc\Delta T$ with $Q$ = the energy stored at full speed ✓
$\Delta T = 58.5\ \text{K}$; allow ECF from (a)(ii) ✓

stem: A weather balloon is filled with helium and released from a ground station. It carries a payload of instruments and a radio transmitter. At launch the balloon has a volume of 4.2 $\text{m}^{3}$ and the total mass of the balloon, helium and payload is 3.1 kg. The density of the air at ground level is 1.2 $\text{kg m}^{-3}$.

parts.label: a(i)
parts.question: Show that the buoyancy force on the balloon at launch is about 49 N.
markscheme: $F_{\text{b}} = \rho V g$ (the weight of the air displaced) ✓
$F_{\text{b}} = 1.2 \times 4.2 \times 9.8 = 49.4\ \text{N}$ ✓

parts.label: a(ii)
parts.question: Calculate the initial acceleration of the balloon.
markscheme: resultant force $= 49.4 - 30.4$ (weight $= mg$) ✓
Allow ECF from (a)(i); accept 5.88 to 6.38 $\text{m s}^{-2}$

mistakes.feedback: The resultant force is the buoyancy force minus the weight of the balloon and payload.

parts.label: a(iii)
parts.question: As the balloon rises, the density of the surrounding air decreases. The helium stays at the same pressure and temperature as the surrounding air. Suggest why the buoyancy force on the balloon stays about the same as it rises.
markscheme: The balloon expands as the air pressure falls, so the volume of air displaced increases ✓
the density of the air and the volume of the balloon change in inverse proportion (both depend on $p/T$), so $\rho V$, the mass of air displaced, and hence the buoyancy force stay about constant ✓

parts.label: b(i)
parts.question: At launch the helium has a pressure of $1.01 \times 10^{5}$ Pa and a temperature of 15 °C. At the highest point of its flight the pressure of the helium is 5500 Pa and its temperature is −56 °C. Calculate the volume of the balloon at the highest point.
markscheme: $\dfrac{p_1V_1}{T_1} = \dfrac{p_2V_2}{T_2}$ with temperatures in kelvin (288 K and 217 K) ✓
Accept 55.7 to 60.5 $\text{m}^{3}$. Award [1 max] for using Celsius temperatures.

mistakes.feedback: The temperature also changes: use pV/T = constant with temperatures in kelvin.

parts.label: b(ii)
parts.question: State one assumption made in your calculation in (b)(i).
markscheme: no helium leaks out / the amount of gas is constant / helium behaves as an ideal gas / the helium is in thermal equilibrium with the air ✓

parts.label: b(iii)
parts.question: Outline why helium is well described by the ideal gas model in these conditions.
markscheme: the pressure (density) is low, so the molecules are far apart compared with their size ✓
the temperature is far above the boiling point of helium, so intermolecular forces are negligible compared with the kinetic energy of the molecules ✓

parts.label: c(i)
parts.question: The radio transmitter has a frequency of 403 MHz. Calculate the wavelength of the radio waves.
markscheme: $\lambda = \dfrac{c}{f} = 0.744\ \text{m}$ ✓

parts.label: c(ii)
